name: Report and investigate incidents
summary: When someone is hurt, nearly hurt, equipment is damaged or fuel is spilled on a project, the foreman gives first aid and reports it, the superintendent secures the area and decides how serious it is, and the safety team records and investigates it. Critical injuries must be phoned in to the provincial ministry at once with a written report within 48 hours, and injuries needing health care or time off go to the workers' compensation board within three business days, while HR arranges modified work. Investigations look for root causes, the safety manager approves corrective actions, and the coordinator closes the case once they are in place. The process is slow when investigations wait for the safety manager's sign-off and when corrective actions need materials or other trades, and error-prone when incidents are reported late or witness statements are thin.

baseline.org_archetype: A national Canadian general contractor acting as constructor on about 220 active projects, covering incidents to its own workers and to subcontractor workers on its sites.
baseline.notes: Incident mix assumed: about 45% near misses, 30% first aid, 15% medical aid or modified work, 3% lost time, 7% property damage or spills; about one critical injury every two to three months.

trigger: A worker, foreman or subcontractor reports an injury, near miss, property damage or spill on a company project.
end_state: The incident is recorded, required regulator and workers' compensation reports are filed, the investigation is approved and its corrective actions are verified and closed.

volume.seasonality: Higher from May to October with more workers and overtime; slips and falls on ice add cases in January and February.

evidence.note: About 1,330 company field workers and several times as many subcontractor workers on company sites; at typical commercial construction rates of a few recordable injuries per 200,000 hours, with first aids and near misses several times the recordables, about 90 reports a month is plausible. Not checked against Bird's published safety statistics.

surge.cause: Summer heat waves causing heat stress cases and fatigue-related incidents

evidence.note: Estimate; heat stress is a common seasonal cause of first aid cases on Ontario and Prairie sites.

resources.name: Pickup trucks for superintendents, foremen and safety staff

steps.name: Report the incident and give first aid
steps.description: The injured worker or a witness tells the foreman, who gives first aid or calls the site first aider, makes the area safe and phones the superintendent; for a near miss the foreman reports what nearly happened.

error.defect_description: Incident reported late, after the shift, or details missing.

control.basis: Company incident reporting procedure: report before the end of the shift

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Secure the area and classify severity
steps.description: The superintendent goes to the location, keeps people away from the scene, checks the worker's condition and classifies the event as near miss, first aid, medical aid, lost time, critical injury, property damage or spill.

error.defect_description: Injury classed as first aid when it later needs medical care, delaying the WSIB report.

next.condition: near miss, first aid, property damage or spill

evidence.note: Severity mix is an estimate; see baseline notes.

steps.name: Notify the ministry and hold the scene
steps.description: The superintendent calls 911 if needed, phones the ministry inspector, the joint health and safety committee or representative and the union immediately, and keeps the scene undisturbed until an inspector allows it to be changed.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA s.51: immediate notice of a death or critical injury and preservation of the scene

evidence.note: CCOHS summarises the Ontario OHSA s.51 duty: immediate telephone notice and a written report within 48 hours for a death or critical injury.

steps.name: Prepare the 48-hour written report
steps.description: The regional safety manager attends the site, collects the facts, photos and witness names, and writes the report to the ministry director with the prescribed details, copying the committee and union, within 48 hours.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA s.51(1): written report to the Director within 48 hours

evidence.note: CCOHS summarises the Ontario OHSA s.51 duty: immediate telephone notice and a written report within 48 hours for a death or critical injury.

steps.name: Drive the injured worker to a clinic
steps.description: The foreman or site first aider drives the worker in a company pickup to the walk-in clinic or hospital emergency department, waits with them, and brings back the treatment and work-restriction form.

control.basis: Workplace Safety and Insurance Act: employer pays transport to first treatment and the day's wages

evidence.note: WSIB requires the employer to pay a full day's wages on the day of the injury; clinic times are estimates.

steps.name: Enter the initial incident report
steps.description: Before the end of the day the superintendent enters the initial report in the safety system: who, where, when, what happened, the immediate cause, first aid given and photos.

error.defect_description: Thin description or missing photos and witnesses.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Gather facts and witness statements
steps.description: The safety coordinator reads the initial report, goes to the location, takes witness statements, photos and measurements, checks the FLHA and training records for the crew, and corrects the severity classification if needed.

next.condition: high-potential near miss or property damage
low-potential near miss or first aid

evidence.note: CCOHS describes team investigations led by people who know the work, root cause tools and management follow-up of corrective actions. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Report the spill and direct clean-up
steps.description: The environmental specialist confirms what spilled and how much, reports it to the provincial spills line when it may affect the environment, and directs the clean-up contractor and disposal records.

control.basis: Ontario Environmental Protection Act spill reporting (Part X) and provincial equivalents

evidence.note: Spill reporting duty named from general knowledge; source not opened. Times are estimates.

steps.name: File the WSIB Form 7
steps.description: The HR and benefits administrator completes the employer's report of injury (Form 7) online from the incident report and clinic form, gives the worker a copy and starts the claim file.

error.defect_description: Late filing or a wrong date of injury or earnings figure.

control.basis: WSIB: employer reports within three business days of learning of the injury

next.condition: lost time or modified work needed

evidence.note: Three-business-day deadline and triggers from WSIB; times are estimates.

steps.name: Arrange modified work and track return to work
steps.description: The HR administrator reads the clinic's work restrictions, agrees suitable modified duties with the superintendent, sends the written offer to the worker and WSIB, and tracks the worker until they return to full duties.

control.basis: Workplace Safety and Insurance Act duty to co-operate in early and safe return to work

evidence.note: WSIB reporting triggers include modified work; return-to-work duties named from general knowledge.

steps.name: Investigate root causes
steps.description: The safety coordinator leads the investigation with the superintendent, the foreman and the committee worker member, rebuilds the sequence of events and asks why each condition existed, then writes causes and proposed corrective actions in the safety system.

error.defect_description: Investigation stops at worker error without finding the system cause.

control.basis: COR incident investigation element: root cause and corrective actions

evidence.note: CCOHS describes team investigations led by people who know the work, root cause tools and management follow-up of corrective actions. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve the investigation and corrective actions
steps.description: The regional safety manager reads the investigation, checks that root causes go beyond the injured worker, and approves the corrective actions, owners and due dates or sends it back.

control.basis: Company incident management procedure: manager sign-off of investigations

next.condition: sent back for deeper root cause

evidence.note: CCOHS describes team investigations led by people who know the work, root cause tools and management follow-up of corrective actions. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Notify the insurer of property damage
steps.description: When a low-potential incident involves property or third-party damage, the safety coordinator sends the incident report and photos to the risk and insurance team for an insurance notice.

evidence.note: Share of incidents needing an insurance notice is folded into the corrective action path; estimate.

steps.name: Review a low-potential incident
steps.description: For a first aid or low-potential near miss, the safety coordinator reviews the facts, records a simple cause and a corrective action such as housekeeping or a toolbox talk, and assigns it to the foreman.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

steps.name: Implement corrective actions on site
steps.description: The superintendent puts the actions in place: guardrails or covers installed, equipment repaired or replaced, a procedure changed, a trade's worker retrained, or a site-wide safety stand-down held.

evidence.note: Waits for materials, rented equipment or a trade's crew; estimate.

steps.name: Share lessons learned
steps.description: The safety coordinator writes a short safety alert or toolbox talk on the incident, sends it to the region's sites and checks that foremen covered it at the next talks.

evidence.note: CCOHS describes team investigations led by people who know the work, root cause tools and management follow-up of corrective actions. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Add the incident to monthly statistics
steps.description: The regional safety manager's monthly report pulls the incident into the injury frequency and severity figures and the list of serious incidents for the operations review.

evidence.note: Monthly batch runs in parallel with the corrective actions; estimate.

steps.name: Verify actions and close the incident
steps.description: The safety coordinator checks on site that each corrective action is in place and working, attaches photos, and closes the incident in the safety system, or re-opens the action if it is missing or ineffective.

control.basis: COR incident investigation element: follow-up of corrective actions

evidence.note: CCOHS describes team investigations led by people who know the work, root cause tools and management follow-up of corrective actions. Minutes are the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Critical injury
exceptions.description: Immediate ministry, committee and union notice, scene held for the inspector, 48-hour written report and WSIB report.

exceptions.name: Lost time or modified work
exceptions.description: WSIB Form 7 within three business days and a modified work offer tracked by HR.

exceptions.name: Spill
exceptions.description: Fuel, hydraulic oil or concrete washout reaches soil or a drain; the environmental specialist reports and directs clean-up.

exceptions.name: Investigation sent back
exceptions.description: The safety manager rejects an investigation that blames the worker without finding the system cause.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from report to incident closed
benchmarks.population: Construction incidents reported on Canadian general contractor projects

evidence.note: Common COR practice targets investigation within a few days and corrective action closure within about 30 days; no published benchmark found.

benchmarks.unit: business days from learning of the injury

pain_points.description: Investigations queue for the regional safety manager's approval, covering dozens of sites each.

evidence.note: Six regional safety managers for about 90 incidents a month; estimate.

pain_points.description: Late or thin first reports leave the coordinator chasing witnesses days later, and injuries first classed as first aid become WSIB cases after the deadline clock has started.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

pain_points.description: Corrective actions wait for materials, rented equipment or the responsible trade, so incidents stay open for weeks.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian general contractor practice under a COR program.

sources.title: Health and Safety Legislation in Canada - Injury Reporting
sources.publisher: Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety
sources.supports: Ontario OHSA s.51: notify an inspector immediately by telephone and send a written report within 48 hours for a death or critical injury; WSIB report within 3 days; Alberta: report serious incidents to a Director as soon as possible and submit the WCB employer report within 72 hours.

sources.title: Incident Investigation
sources.publisher: Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety
sources.supports: Investigation by a team including the supervisor, workers and a committee member; start as soon as possible, secure the scene and identify witnesses; look for root causes with tools such as 5 Whys; management assigns corrective actions with a timetable and monitors completion; committee can monitor progress.

sources.title: Report an injury or illness
sources.supports: Employer reports on Form 7 within three business days when a worker needs health care beyond first aid, loses time or pay, or needs modified work at regular pay for more than seven days; give the worker a copy; penalties for late reporting.

assumptions: Ontario rules (OHSA s.51, WSIB Form 7) are used as the reference; Alberta requires serious incidents to be reported to a Director as soon as possible and the WCB employer report within 72 hours, which gives similar timing.
Step s13 (insurance notice) is reached only from low-potential property damage cases; higher-value damage claims are handled in legal-insurance-claims after s11.
The ministry inspector's visit and any orders after a critical injury belong to hse-ministry-inspection and are not modelled here.
WSIB claim adjudication and long return-to-work cases continue after the incident is closed and are not part of the cycle time.
The foreman, environmental specialist and HR administrator take part although the process map lists only the safety coordinator, safety manager, superintendent and HR administrator.
Loaded costs and shift patterns come from the organisation file.
